sentences.text: The remains consist of a partial postcranial skeleton preserving most hindlimbs, an almost complete forelimb, and tail vertebrae.
Its body was slender, with long, thin limbs giving it a gracile appearance.
The proximal carpal bones of the forearm are relatively short and stout, measuring more than a quarter of their maximum length.
These proximal carpals are at most one-tenth the length of the corresponding forearm bones.
A double row of paramedian osteoderms covered the back, a condition shared with other early crocodylomorphs.
Each osteoderm is elongated, being about 2.5 times longer than wide.
The armor plates are leaf-shaped or subrectangular, with a straight inner edge and a curved outer edge that ends in a spike-like process.
Their surface bears shallow pits surrounding a long keel that runs along the middle.
Overall, it is interpreted as a small, slender terrestrial quadruped adopting an erect posture.
Elongated proximal carpals formed a single functional unit designed to support the animal’s weight.
The first metacarpal is shortened, indicating that the associated digit likely did not bear weight while the animal stood.
A relatively high metatarsal-to-femur ratio suggests it could run faster than its close relative.
Its limb proportions point to a fast-running, digitigrade stance on land.
The holotype was recovered by Ron Croucher in 1969.
It came from site 1 of the fissure deposits at Cromhall Quarry in Gloucestershire, southwest England.
The specimen is catalogued as NHMUK PV R 10002.
The find consists of a partially articulated postcranial skeleton, a nearly complete right forelimb, isolated osteoderms and ribs, and remains of a rhynchocephalian reptile.
Cromhall Quarry, also called Slickstones Quarry, is a Late Triassic to Early Jurassic fissure deposit in the Bristol Channel area.
The type locality is Cromhall Quarry, and the fossils were discovered in the United Kingdom.
The species was described from this semi-articulated partial postcranial skeleton found at the quarry.
The reduced fifth metacarpal resembles the first digit, differing from the condition in Terrestrisuchus.
It belongs to the order Crocodylomorpha and the family Saltoposuchidae.
Phylogenetic work by Bodenham and colleagues placed it within Saltoposuchidae.
Analyses recover it as the sister taxon of Terrestrisuchus.
It is classified in the clade Saltoposuchidae and is the sister taxon to Terrestrisuchus.
The genus and species were formally named Galahadosuchus jonesi.
It lived during the Late Triassic, spanning the Carnian to Rhaetian stages.
It is an extinct saltoposuchid crocodylomorph known from fissure deposits of that age in the United Kingdom.
Its fossils come from Late Triassic fissure deposits of the Bristol Channel area in southwest England and south Wales.
Researchers discuss whether different weighting methods in phylogenetic analysis alter its placement within Saltoposuchidae.
There is debate over whether humerus proportions suggest it was less capable of terrestrial movement, noting possible biases from including modern crocodiles in datasets.
The idea that the shortened first digit did not bear weight is based on the reduced first metacarpal, a point of contention among specialists.
